# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 13 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Disagreement 1 — WIS 13:1: "Vain by nature" vs. "foolish by nature" — mataioi

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "Vain by nature are all who are ignorant of God" |
| LOGOS | "All who were ignorant of God were foolish by nature" |
| PNEUMA | "All people who remain ignorant of God are simply foolish" |

**Issue:** Greek mataioi physei — "vain/empty by nature." Mataios in LXX usage often translates Hebrew hebel ("vanity/breath," as in Ecclesiastes). It can mean "vain" (morally empty), "foolish" (practically without understanding), or "futile" (intellectually null). EMET's "vain" preserves the LXX register; LOGOS's "foolish" is cleaner in English; PNEUMA adds "simply" which editorializes. The parallel with Romans 1:21 ("their thinking became futile" — emataiōthēsan) supports "vain/futile" over "foolish."

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "All who were ignorant of God were foolish by nature" (LOGOS). While "vain" has stronger LXX resonance, "foolish" is more immediately intelligible in this didactic context. A footnote to the LXX/Romans parallel is warranted.

---

## Disagreement 2 — WIS 13:1: "the One-Who-Is" — ho ōn

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "could not know the One-Who-Is" |
| LOGOS | "to know the One Who Is" |
| PNEUMA | "to know the One Who Truly Is" |

**Issue:** Greek ton onta — "the one who is/exists" — a participial phrase that uses the LXX's rendering of the divine name from Exodus 3:14 (egō eimi ho ōn, "I am the One Who Is"). This is philosophically loaded: the true God is defined by being/existence in a way that created things are not. EMET capitalizes the whole epithet; LOGOS capitalizes "One Who Is"; PNEUMA adds "Truly" which is an interpretive addition but philosophically defensible.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "to know the One Who Is" (LOGOS). The Exodus 3:14 allusion must be preserved through capitalization. PNEUMA's "Truly" adds what is already implied but risks weakening the technical force of the participial form.

---

## Disagreement 3 — WIS 13:5: "proportionately seen" vs. "correspondingly perceived" — analogōs

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "their Creator is proportionately seen" |
| LOGOS | "their Creator is correspondingly perceived" |
| PNEUMA | "you can catch a proportional glimpse of their Creator" |

**Issue:** Greek analogōs theōreitai — "by analogy is contemplated/seen." This is an argument from analogy — the philosophical method of reasoning from effects to causes by proportion. EMET's "proportionately seen" and LOGOS's "correspondingly perceived" both work; PNEUMA's "catch a glimpse" weakens the philosophical precision. "Theōreitai" is the philosophical term for intellectual contemplation (theōria).

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "their Creator is correspondingly perceived" (LOGOS). "Correspondingly" captures the analogical method; "perceived" (rather than "seen") preserves the intellectual/contemplative character of theōria. This verse is the most philosophically precise moment in ch. 13 and deserves precision.

---

## Disagreement 4 — WIS 13:6: Partial excuse — "lesser blame" vs. "moderate blame" vs. "somewhat less"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "a lesser blame is due" |
| LOGOS | "the blame is somewhat less" |
| PNEUMA | "deserve only a moderate blame" |

**Issue:** Greek esti gar autois touto mikrikon tō memphthenai — "for to these [ones] there is this [thing]: to be blamed in a small way." The natural worshippers (stars, elements) get partial credit for genuine seeking; the idol-makers of vv.10-19 get no credit. EMET's "lesser blame" implies comparison; LOGOS's "somewhat less" softens appropriately; PNEUMA's "moderate" is a paraphrase.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "the blame is somewhat less" (LOGOS). The graduated scale of culpability is key to the chapter's argument and "somewhat less" captures the limited mitigation the author allows.

---

## Disagreement 5 — WIS 13:10: "likenesses of animals" — the idol catalogue

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "gold and silver, products-of-skill, and likenesses of animals, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand" |
| LOGOS | "gold and silver, craft of skill, and likenesses of animals, or a useless stone, the work of some ancient craftsman" |
| PNEUMA | "gold, silver, clever craft-work, likenesses of animals, or some useless stone chiseled out by some craftsman long ago" |

**Issue:** The idol catalogue here distinguishes natural-material idols (gold, silver), crafted animal-likenesses (Egyptian gods), and stone idols (Canaanite masseboth?). EMET's "products-of-skill" and LOGOS's "craft of skill" both render technēs erga; LOGOS's "some ancient craftsman" is slightly better than EMET's "an ancient hand" since the point is human craft, not the hand alone. PNEUMA's "clever" editorializes.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "gold and silver, craft of skill, and likenesses of animals, or a useless stone, the work of some ancient craftsman" (LOGOS). Clean and precise.

---

## Disagreement 6 — WIS 13:11-15: The woodcutter parable — structure and tone

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | Translated as a continuous run-on sentence |
| LOGOS | Broken into discrete actions with clear antecedent "remainder" for v.13 |
| PNEUMA | Broken into short dramatic beats; "Imagine a woodcutter..." |

**Issue:** The Greek woodcutter parable (vv.11-15) is a single extended period (periodos) — one long grammatical sentence describing a sequence of events. EMET preserves this as an unbroken structure; LOGOS breaks it into readable sub-units; PNEUMA restructures it as a dramatic narrative vignette. The author's point is the absurdity of the sequence — the idol is a leftover byproduct of practical woodwork. The comic irony depends on following the whole sequence.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS. Breaking the extended period into recognizable clauses while maintaining the sequential logic serves English readers without losing the rhetorical point.

---

## Disagreement 7 — WIS 13:17-19: The fourfold irony — lifeless, powerless, dead, inexperienced

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "a lifeless [thing]... a thing without-strength... a dead [thing]... an utterly inexperienced [thing]... a thing having hands without-strength" |
| LOGOS | "a lifeless thing... the powerless... the dead... the wholly inexperienced... a thing whose hands have no effectiveness" |
| PNEUMA | "this dead thing... something without any strength... a corpse... something that has never had a moment of experience... something whose own hands are utterly incapable" |

**Issue:** The four parallel contrasts (life/health/aid/journey prayed for from a lifeless/powerless/dead/inexperienced thing) form a tight rhetorical chiasm. PNEUMA's "corpse" is vivid but is a different word — the Greek nekrōi means "dead one" (a dead thing), not specifically a corpse. LOGOS preserves the four-part parallelism cleanly.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS for all four clauses. The fourfold parallelism is the author's rhetorical climax and must be preserved with consistent grammatical structure. "The dead," "the wholly inexperienced," and "the powerless" as parallel objects of entreaty make the absurdity clear.
